summary: A first-person account of how augmented reality, introduced via Microsoft HoloLens 2 after September 1, 2023, changed collaboration, training, and remote work at the author's company. It covers milestones from the first AR training to a factory emergency repair, along with cost savings, converted skeptics, and data security challenges. The author concludes AR has become a staple of daily work with further potential.
one_line: A first-person account of adopting Microsoft HoloLens 2 AR at work, improving collaboration, training, remote work and repair, while managing security concerns.
key_facts: The author's team first encountered AR on a Monday morning not long after September 1, 2023, when manager David Skinner introduced the Microsoft HoloLens 2.
Sarah Bennet, a senior architect, rotated a 3D model of a building in AR so the team could inspect it without printing a physical blueprint.

The first AR training session took place around mid-September, led by a virtual expert projected into the meeting room, where engineers assembled a complex machine part with floating instructions and lit-up tools.
On October 5, project lead Jack Morrison organized an AR-powered design workshop; he said "AR has not only bridged our thoughts but our spirits too!"

The headquarters in Chicago and a satellite office in Singapore held holographic meetings; on November 6, Dr. Rachel Lui in Singapore diagnosed a machine in real time while the author observed from Chicago.

By early December, reduced travel costs, printed materials and training machine downtime won over skeptics in the finance department despite the high initial investment in AR gear and software development.
CFO Martin Green said the return on investment with AR was faster than anticipated: "The future doesn't seem so distant when you're already reaping its rewards."
During an emergency factory-floor maintenance issue on January 15, technicians wore AR headsets showing repair procedures over the machinery, and downtime was reduced by half.
Skeptic Anne Garret, who once dismissed AR as a fad, led a complex virtual staff training session in February and became an advocate, teaching a newbie to operate a CNC machine through AR.
Data security and privacy concerns arose with cloud-based AR applications; the IT department led by Leo Thompson secured all AR interactions with end-to-end encryption.
Leo Thompson stressed the need to embrace innovation while protecting intellectual property and employee privacy.
